questions.question: A Streptococcus pyogenes isolate is tested as resistant to penicillin.
questions.question_raw: A Streptococcus pyogenes isolate is tested as resistant to penicillin.

parts.text: What are 5 things you can do to verify this result?

parts_raw.text: What are 5 things you can do to verify this result?

questions.model_answer: Penicillin resistance has never been documented in group A Streptococcus, so an apparently resistant result should be treated as an error until confirmed: (1) Re-confirm organism identification — verify it is truly S. pyogenes (β-hemolysis, Lancefield group A carbohydrate/serogrouping, PYR positive) and not another organism. (2) Confirm the culture is pure and not mixed/contaminated, then repeat testing from a fresh subculture. (3) Repeat susceptibility testing by a validated reference method (broth microdilution or gradient MIC strip) rather than relying on the initial result. (4) Check for technical/methodologic error — disk potency and expiry, inoculum density, correct medium, incubation conditions, and reading, and confirm QC strains are in range. (5) Refer the isolate to a reference laboratory for confirmatory MIC testing and re-identification.
questions.beyond_mandell: Steps 2-5 reflect standard CLSI/reference-laboratory quality-control practice; Mandell supports only that penicillin-resistant GAS has never been detected.

questions.model_answer: a) Urgent surgical exploration with direct visualization of necrotic fascia (non-bleeding grey fascia, easy blunt dissection, dishwater fluid) is diagnostic; send intra-operative tissue for Gram stain and culture. b) Piperacillin-tazobactam (or a carbapenem) PLUS vancomycin PLUS clindamycin; once group A streptococcus is confirmed, penicillin G plus clindamycin. c) Gram-positive cocci in chains indicate group A streptococcus — contact plus droplet precautions until 24 h of effective antibiotic therapy. d) For an anaphylactic contact: clindamycin (lincosamide) and azithromycin/clarithromycin (macrolide) — two different classes, avoiding beta-lactams.

questions.model_answer: a) Prompt surgical exploration is the diagnostic gold standard: direct visualization shows swollen, dull grey necrotic superficial fascia, thin "dishwater" exudate, loss of normal resistance so tissue planes separate easily on blunt/finger dissection, and tissue that does not bleed; send tissue for Gram stain, culture and histopathology. Cutaneous anesthesia over the area and pain out of proportion are bedside clues; CT/MRI may support but must never delay operative exploration. b) Broad empiric cover: vancomycin (MRSA) PLUS piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem (gram-negative/anaerobe cover) PLUS clindamycin (antitoxin effect – suppresses streptococcal exotoxin production). c) Gram-positive cocci in chains indicate group A streptococcus: institute contact plus droplet precautions until the patient has received at least 24 hours of effective antimicrobial therapy. d) With true penicillin anaphylaxis (avoid cephalosporins): (1) azithromycin (macrolide) and (2) clindamycin (lincosamide).
questions.beyond_mandell: NF infection-control precautions (part c) and invasive-GAS household post-exposure chemoprophylaxis agents (part d) are not in this chapter slice; they follow CDC/PHAC invasive group A streptococcal contact guidance.

cohort_answer.text: Confirm diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis from surgical intervention - rapidly progressive, pain out of proportion, dishwater fluid appearance when fascia is entered surgically. The fascia at time of direct visual examination is swollen and dull gray with stringy areas of necrosis; a thin, brownish exudate may be present. Empiric regimen: Piperacillin-Tazobactam, Vancomycin, Clindamycin. Precautions: Contact and droplet until on appropriate therapy for 24 hours. Post-exposure prophylaxis: Azithromycin 500mg PO daily x5/7; Clindamycin 300mg PO TID x10/7; PCN dosing 250mg PO QID x10/7

parts_raw.text: List TWO mechanisms of resistance to this antibiotic.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Ribosomal target-site modification — erm-gene-encoded 23S rRNA methylase producing the MLSB phenotype (macrolide–lincosamide–streptogramin B cross-resistance, constitutive or inducible). (2) Active drug efflux — mef-gene-encoded macrolide efflux pump (M phenotype), conferring macrolide resistance while sparing clindamycin.
b) A D-test (erythromycin–clindamycin double-disk induction test) to detect inducible clindamycin resistance, since erm-mediated inducible MLSB isolates can appear clindamycin-susceptible but fail on therapy.
questions.beyond_mandell: Macrolide resistance mechanisms and the D-test are standard CLSI microbiology, not detailed in this Mandell chapter.

questions.model_answer:
a) Any two of: (1) renal impairment; (2) coagulopathy/DIC (thrombocytopenia); (3) liver involvement (elevated transaminases/bilirubin); (4) ARDS; (5) generalized erythematous macular rash that may desquamate; (6) soft-tissue necrosis (necrotizing fasciitis, myositis, or gangrene).
b) Close/household contacts of a confirmed severe invasive GAS case (including STSS or necrotizing fasciitis) who had significant contact during the window from ~7 days before to 24 h after the case started antibiotics.
c) A first-generation cephalosporin (e.g., cephalexin) — or penicillin.
d) Avoid all β-lactams; offer clindamycin (or a macrolide such as azithromycin).
e) (1) Near-universal GAS susceptibility with negligible resistance, versus rising clindamycin resistance among GAS (and no inducible-resistance/D-test pitfall); (2) it likewise suppresses exotoxin production while offering reliable oral bioavailability.
questions.beyond_mandell: Parts b-e (contact prophylaxis criteria, agent choice, and linezolid-versus-clindamycin comparison) rest on CDC/public-health invasive-GAS guidance, not this chapter; only the STSS case-definition criteria (part a) are from Mandell.

questions.model_answer: a) Repeated GAS throat isolation = asymptomatic chronic carrier: no prophylaxis routinely; treat/eradicate only in specific settings (household/institutional outbreaks, recurrent pharyngitis in close contacts, outbreaks of rheumatic fever or post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis). b) Shared a cigarette (exposure to oral secretions) within the week before onset: yes — this is a close contact; give chemoprophylaxis (e.g., ceftriaxone 250 mg IM x1, or rifampin/ciprofloxacin). c) Contact of pneumococcal pneumonia: no chemoprophylaxis; person-to-person prophylaxis is not indicated — consider appropriate pneumococcal vaccination based on age/comorbidity.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only part (b) is grounded in this chapter. GAS carrier management (a) and pneumococcal contact management (c) rest on standard IDSA/GAS and pneumococcal guidance, not this Neisseria chapter.

cohort_answer.text:
Chronic GAS carrier (asymptomatic) = no. Ppx offered if part of institutional outbreak, outbreaks of acute rheumatic fever/post strep GN, infections recurring in household/close contacts. Cephalexin 250mg QID x10 days, Amox 500mg BID x10 days, Erythromycin 250mg QID x10 days (if ceph allergic), Penicillin 300mg VK QID x10 days (alt)
Incubation period of Meningococcus is 1-10 days, usually less than 4 days. IPAC uses 7 days before illness onset as relevant duration. Exposure to oral secretions confers risk, no duration needed, therefore yes. Would give ceftriaxone 250 mg IM x1
Prophylaxis not routinely recommended. Would consider age and medical condition: appropriate pneumococcal vaccination

questions.question_raw:

parts.text: Describe the effects of the toxin (i.e., superantigen).

parts_raw.text: B) Describe the effects of the toxin (ie. Superantigen)

questions.model_answer: Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins act as superantigens: they cause fever, enhance susceptibility to endotoxin, and suppress IgM antibody synthesis. As superantigens they bind simultaneously to class II MHC on antigen-presenting cells and to the V-β region of the T-cell receptor, triggering massive T-cell activation. The net effect is induction of monocyte cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6) and lymphokines (TNF-β, IL-2, IFN-γ), producing the cytokine storm that drives shock and organ failure.

cohort_answer.text: Pyrogenic exotoxins (scarlatina toxins, erythrotoxins) cause fever, enhance susceptibility to endotoxin, suppress IgM antibody synthesis, and act as superantigens. Can stimulate T-cell responses by binding to both MHC class II APC's and to the T-cell receptor itself. Causes induction of monocyte cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6), and lymphokines (TNF-beta, IL-2, and interferon-gamma)

parts.text: List the antibiotics that are used and give the rationale for their use.

parts_raw.text: C) List the antibiotics that are used and give rationale for their use

questions.model_answer: High-dose penicillin PLUS clindamycin. Rationale: (1) Penicillin — all strains of GAS remain susceptible to it, giving reliable bactericidal killing. (2) Clindamycin — a protein-synthesis inhibitor that suppresses production of streptococcal exotoxins and M protein, and its efficacy is not reduced by large inoculum or stationary-phase growth (overcoming the “Eagle effect,” in which penicillin is less effective at high organism density). Clindamycin also dampens host cytokine production. Penicillin is added because clindamycin is bacteriostatic and rare clindamycin resistance can occur.
questions.beyond_mandell: The Eagle-effect/inoculum rationale for clindamycin is established Mandell teaching; the antibiotic combination and toxin-suppression rationale are grounded in the cited page.

cohort_answer.text: Penicillin - all strains of GAS susceptible to penicillin; less effective during stationary growth phase (Eagle effect). Clindamycin - suppresses exotoxin and protein M production at ribosome; suppresses cytokine production by human mononuclear cells (also: Penicillin - bactericidal effect; Clindamycin - bacteriostatic anti-toxinic effect + inoculum effect)

parts.text: The patient's wife asks whether she is at risk for invasive group A streptococcal (GAS) infection compared with the general population. What do you tell her?

parts_raw.text: D) Wife asks whether she is at risk for invasive GAS compared with general population. What do you tell her?

questions.model_answer: a) Reassure her that household contacts of an invasive GAS case are at increased risk relative to the general population, but the absolute risk remains very low. Epidemiologic data show roughly one secondary invasive case among more than 1500 contacts (extrapolating to about 66 per 100,000 contacts per year), versus a primary invasive-disease incidence of about 3.5 per 100,000 per year in the general population, i.e. the risk to contacts is roughly 20 times greater but still very low. Because of this low absolute risk and the lack of a clearly effective chemoprophylactic regimen, routine screening and antibiotic prophylaxis are NOT recommended for household contacts. Prophylaxis is considered selectively for high-risk contacts (open wounds, recent surgery, recent childbirth, concurrent varicella or influenza, immunodeficiency, older age, or comorbidities such as diabetes/cardiac disease/cancer/corticosteroid use). If prophylaxis is given, agents achieving the highest pharyngeal-eradication rates (clindamycin or azithromycin) are chosen.
questions.beyond_mandell: PHAC/CDC guidance provides the operational close-contact definition and specific prophylaxis regimens (e.g., first-generation cephalosporin such as cephalexin); Mandell states specific regimens are published elsewhere and favours clindamycin/azithromycin.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort states the contact risk is 200-2000x the general population; the Mandell text puts it at roughly 20-fold higher (about 66 vs 3.5 per 100,000/yr).

cohort_answer.text: Risk of invasive GAS is 200-2000x higher than general population, but remains rare (3.2/1000). Ppx to close contacts if exposed from 7d prior to sx onset until 24h after starting abx. Definition of close contact given (4h/day average in previous 7 days, or 20h/week; shared bed/sexual relations; mucous membrane contact; shared needles; certain child care/hospital contacts). PHAC recommends cephalexin x 10 days; 2nd line azithromycin x5 or clindamycin x10; 3rd line benzyl penicillin + rifampin x4 days

parts.text: Name two mechanisms of erythromycin (macrolide) resistance in Streptococcus pyogenes.
The isolate demonstrates clindamycin susceptibility. What test do you have to do to confirm this?

parts_raw.text: Name 2 mechanisms (1)
It demonstrates clindamycin susceptibility. What test do you have to do to confirm this (0.5)

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Ribosomal target-site modification: methylation of the 23S rRNA by an erm gene (erm(B)/erm(A)/erm(TR)), producing the MLSB phenotype (macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin B cross-resistance), which may be constitutive or inducible. (2) Active efflux: a mef gene (mef(A))-encoded macrolide efflux pump conferring the M phenotype (macrolide resistance with retained clindamycin susceptibility).
b) Inducible clindamycin resistance testing by the D-zone test (double-disk diffusion, erythromycin disk adjacent to clindamycin disk). It is performed on isolates that are erythromycin-resistant but clindamycin-susceptible; blunting of the clindamycin zone toward the erythromycin disk (a D shape) indicates inducible erm-mediated MLSB resistance and predicts clindamycin failure.
questions.beyond_mandell: This Mandell chapter documents macrolide resistance rates but does not detail the resistance mechanisms or the D-zone test; the mechanisms and inducible-clindamycin (D-test) methodology are from standard CLSI/clinical microbiology guidance.

cohort_answer.text: Mechanisms: Alteration in the ribosomal target site or efflux pumps (Mandell's) - mefA efflux pump (specific to strep, other names for staph); MLSB (macrolide lincosamide streptogramin B) resistance from ribosomal methylation altering ribosomal binding site, can be constitutive or inducible (induced by erythromycin exposure making resistant to clindamycin via inducible erm gene). Test: Do inducible clindamycin resistance testing (D-zone test) - only used for Staph species, S. pneumoniae, and beta-hemolytic streptococci; only performed in isolates erythromycin resistant and clindamycin susceptible; detects erm gene-mediated resistance (ribosomal methylation); confers MLSB phenotype

questions.model_answer: (1) Target-site modification: methylation of the 23S rRNA (domain V, adenine A2058) by a ribosomal methylase, reducing binding of macrolides, lincosamides and streptogramin B (MLS-B phenotype); gene = erm (ermB in S. pneumoniae, ermB/ermTR/ermA in GAS); clindamycin resistance = YES (constitutive MLS-B) - may be inducible and detected by D-test. (2) Active efflux: an ATP-driven/major-facilitator efflux pump exports 14- and 15-membered macrolides only (M phenotype), sparing 16-membered macrolides, clindamycin and streptogramins; gene = mef (mefA/mefE in S. pneumoniae, mefA in GAS); clindamycin resistance = NO.

questions.model_answer: a) Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) and Streptococcus pyogenes (group A streptococcus) — purulence points to S. aureus/MRSA. b) Doxycycline — covers MRSA, streptococci, and Vibrio vulnificus in a single oral agent. c) Two alternative regimens each covering MRSA + streptococcus + Vibrio: (1) Ceftriaxone 1 g IV once daily (Vibrio, streptococci, MSSA) PLUS trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole BID PO (MRSA); (2) Ciprofloxacin BID PO (Vibrio/gram-negatives) PLUS linezolid 600 mg BID PO (MRSA, streptococci). d) (1) Vibrio vulnificus (2) Aeromonas hydrophila (3) Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae (4) Mycobacterium marinum (5) Streptococcus iniae (Edwardsiella tarda also acceptable).
questions.beyond_mandell: Specific combination regimens to cover MRSA plus Vibrio reflect IDSA SSTI guidance applied to the chapter's pathogen list.

questions.question: A person has a fluctuant mass in his neck with erythema, swelling and tenderness. For each scenario, name the most common pathogen and the most appropriate specimen and microbiologic test.
questions.question_raw: Person has a fluctuant mass in his neck with erythema, swelling and tenderness. For the following scenarios, name the most common pathogen and the most appropriate specimen and microbiologic test.

parts.text: Recently ate steak tartare.
Immigrant from Vietnam, also has cough and weight loss over a few weeks.
Bitten by a rabbit on the shoulder.
Inflamed tonsils with exudate.

parts_raw.text: Recently ate steak tartar
Immigrant from Vietnam, also has cough and weight loss over few weeks
Bit by a rabbit on the shoulder
Inflamed tonsils with exudate

questions.model_answer:
a) Toxoplasma gondii; specimen: serum; test: Toxoplasma IgG/IgM serology (acute and convalescent). [Beyond this chapter.]
b) Mycobacterium tuberculosis (cervical scrofula); specimen: fine-needle aspirate or excisional lymph node biopsy; test: AFB smear, mycobacterial culture and NAAT. [Beyond this chapter.]
c) Francisella tularensis (ulceroglandular tularemia); specimen: serum (organism rarely seen/grown, and culture is hazardous); test: tube- or micro-agglutination serology, acute and convalescent (fourfold rise); node aspirate can be sent for PCR/culture on cysteine-enriched media at a reference lab under BSL-3.
d) Streptococcus pyogenes; specimen: throat swab; test: rapid antigen and/or throat culture. [Beyond this chapter.]
questions.beyond_mandell: Parts a, b and d (Toxoplasma, TB adenitis, S. pyogenes) are outside the Francisella chapter; answered from standard ID knowledge (Mandell relevant chapters/IDSA).

cohort_answer.text: Steak tartar: Toxoplasma gondii. Blood serology acute and convalescent. Immigrant from Vietnam: Tuberculosis adenitis - fine needle aspiration or excisional biopsy for AFB and mycobacterial culture. Rabbit bite: Francisella tularensis, blood serology at time of presentation and 2-4 weeks after. Inflamed tonsils: Strep pyogenes. Pharyngeal culture. Parapharyngeal/retropharyngeal collection may need to be drained and can be cultured
